Class StepBack

java.lang.Object
dev.swordai.core.rl.StepBack
public final class StepBack extends Object
After a hit of its own that has not sent the opponent away, it steps back out of that opponent's reach until its sword is nearly back, and only then comes in again.

What that is for. A hit throws the opponent up for four or five ticks and it comes down for as many. If it was thrown back as well, it comes down three or four blocks off and there is nothing it can do. If it was not (a server that hands out part of the knockback, a jump made with the hit, a wall behind it, a critical hit, which knocks back little), it comes down within a sword's reach of a fighter whose own sword is still on its way back, and the hit it makes on the way down is a critical one: the punish crit, which this fighter makes itself (AnswerRule). There is no swing to answer it with, and none is made early. What there is: not to be there. Walking backwards covers a block and a half in the time the opponent is in the air, and an opponent in the air cannot follow.

Which opponent that is, it finds out by being hit so (wary): hit three to thirteen ticks after a hit of its own, with its sword on the way back, twice within five seconds. From then on, for as long as that goes on, it steps back from every hit on the tick it lands, before there is anything to read, and goes after the opponent again if the hit turns out to have sent it flying. Against anyone else it does not step back at all: that costs the ticks its own combos, and its chase of an opponent that runs, are made of.

What was measured, the network not learning, against the opponent that answers every hit on its way down: without this, 77 hits landed and 77 taken a minute, 62 of those taken such answers; with it, 59 landed and 52 taken, 23 of them such answers. (Only stepping back from an opponent known to answer, and not on what can be read, was tried for half an hour of training: 67 and 73.)

Backing off is what a player who follows with a running jump is waiting for (JumpReset). Here the opponent is in the air from the hit and cannot take one; by the time it can, the sword is back, and an opponent that jumps then is run at and hit on its way up (MeetJump).

Read from what the network is shown. Not thread-safe; one per fighter.
